opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think we're not quite there yet, but we're closer than people sometimes assume, and the gap matters in specific ways.

On the one hand, interpretability has made real progress. We can find features inside models that correspond to meaningful concepts, we can trace circuits for certain behaviors, and with causal methods like interventions and steering we can sometimes show that a particular internal mechanism is actually responsible for an output, not just correlated with it. That's a big step up from where the field was five or six years ago, when a lot of the work was basically making pretty pictures of attention heads and telling stories about them.

But if you're asking whether a regulator could say "before you deploy this model, prove to us using interpretability that it doesn't have dangerous capability X or deceptive tendency Y," we can't do that reliably today. Our methods tend to work well on narrow, well-defined behaviors, and they get much shakier when you scale up to the full complexity of a frontier model. We also don't have great ways to measure completeness. If I find a circuit, how do I know I've found all of the mechanism and not just the part that was easiest to see? Without that, you can't really make guarantees, and regulation tends to want guarantees, or at least auditable standards.

So where I think interpretability can be useful right now is less as a certification tool and more as part of the evidence base. It can help with auditing and red-teaming, generating hypotheses about failure modes, checking whether a safety fine-tune actually changed the underlying mechanism or just suppressed the surface behavior. That's genuinely valuable for policymakers to understand, even if it isn't a pass/fail test.

The other thing I'd push for is that regulation shouldn't hard-code specific interpretability techniques, because the field is moving fast and today's best method could look naive in two years. What would help more is investment in standardized benchmarks for evaluating interpretability methods themselves, so that when we do say "this model has been audited," that claim actually means something. And access matters a lot too: a lot of this work requires model weights, so whether independent researchers can audit models, rather than just the labs themselves, is probably one of the more important policy questions in this space.

r001.rationale: The response says interpretability can help policymakers understand model behavior and support auditing and red-teaming.

r002.rationale: It says interpretability cannot reliably certify dangerous capabilities or tendencies today, and argues for benchmarks and evidence rather than treating current methods as a regulatory pass/fail standard.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think we're much less ready than the hype would suggest, and I say that as someone who works on this stuff and really believes in it.

Let me separate two things. There's interpretability as a scientific program, where we try to understand what's actually happening inside these models mechanistically, and then there's interpretability as a tool you could hand to a regulator and say, "run this, and it'll tell you whether the model is safe." Those are very different maturity levels. The science has made real progress. We can find features, we can trace some circuits, we can do interventions that change behavior in predictable ways. But the gap between "we found a neat circuit for this one behavior in this one model" and "we can certify that a frontier model doesn't have some property" is enormous.

The core problem is that our methods are still mostly descriptive rather than predictive. If you ask me, "does this model have a deceptive tendency," I can go looking, and I might find something interesting, but I can't give you a guarantee about absence. And regulation usually wants something closer to a guarantee, or at least a reliable, reproducible test. Right now our tools have a lot of researcher degrees of freedom. Two groups could look at the same model and tell you different stories, and both would be partially right.

There's also a scaling issue. A lot of the cleanest interpretability results are on small models or toy settings. The methods that do scale, like sparse autoencoders or probing, give you a lot of pieces, but assembling those into a holistic understanding of a model with hundreds of billions of parameters is not something we know how to do yet. So if a regulator asked, "give me an interpretability audit of this model," I genuinely don't know what the deliverable would look like.

That said, I don't think the right conclusion is "interpretability has nothing to offer regulation." I think it's more that the near-term role should be modest and honest. Interpretability can inform behavioral evaluations, it can help you understand why an eval failed, it can flag things worth investigating further. Those are real contributions. And regulation can push on the research side, for instance by requiring some level of model access for independent researchers, which is a prerequisite for any of this to work at all.

What I worry about is the opposite failure mode, where interpretability gets treated as a kind of safety theater. A company says "we did an interpretability analysis," a regulator checks a box, and nobody has actually learned anything about whether the model is safe. That would be bad for the field and bad for the public. So my pitch is: regulators should take interpretability seriously as something to invest in and build toward, but they should be skeptical of anyone claiming it's ready today to serve as the primary basis for a compliance regime. It's a five-to-ten-year bet, not a plug-in solution.

r001.rationale: It describes interpretability as a tool regulators could use to assess models and says it can help explain behavior and failed evaluations.

r002.rationale: It says current methods cannot reliably certify model properties and warns that interpretability is not ready to serve as the primary basis for a compliance regime.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s promising, but we’re still quite far from using interpretability as a reliable basis for regulation. There’s a gap between finding an interesting mechanism in a model and being able to say, “We’ve inspected this system, and we know it’s safe.” We shouldn’t confuse those two things.

If you find a mechanism that produces a dangerous behavior, that can be useful evidence. But if you don’t find one, it might just mean your tools aren’t good enough to detect it. That makes interpretability a difficult foundation for a safety certification right now.

I’d be more comfortable using it as one source of evidence alongside behavioral testing and monitoring. And regulation can help make that research possible—for example, by giving independent researchers access to models. The near-term role is supporting investigations and improving our understanding, rather than providing a definitive stamp of approval.

r001.rationale: It says interpretability can support investigations and improve understanding, but does not identify equipping regulators to understand model behavior as a goal.

r002.rationale: It says interpretability is not yet a reliable basis for regulation or safety certification, but does not specifically state that current findings cannot confidently be used directly to formulate new laws.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d say it’s ready to inform regulation, but not ready to serve as the foundation for it. Interpretability can help us investigate how a model produces a particular behavior and identify possible failure modes. But we can’t yet look inside a model and reliably certify that it’s safe.

The distinction is between finding evidence of a problem and proving the absence of one. If an interpretability method reveals a concerning mechanism, that could be useful evidence. If it doesn’t find anything, that might simply mean the method missed it.

So I’d encourage regulators to support interpretability research and access for independent researchers, while grounding current requirements in behavioral evaluations, deployment safeguards, and incident reporting. Interpretability should contribute to that evidence, without becoming a stamp of approval that promises more than the science can deliver.

r001.rationale: It says interpretability can help investigate how models produce behavior and recommends supporting regulators’ use of that research.

r002.rationale: It says interpretability is ready to inform regulation but not to serve as its foundation, and explains that current methods cannot reliably certify safety.
